content: Berberis vulgaris, commonly known as European Barberry, is a deciduous shrub belonging to the family Berberidaceae. It is native to central and southern Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia. The plant has also become naturalized in northern Europe, including the British Isles and Scandinavia, as well as in North America. This shrub can grow up to a height of 4 meters. Its leaves are small, oval-shaped, measuring 2 to 5 cm in length and 1 to 2 cm in width, with serrated edges. These leaves are typically grouped in clusters of 2 to 5 and are subtended by a three-branched spine that is 3 to 8 mm long. The flowers of Berberis vulgaris are yellow, measuring 4 to 6 mm in diameter, and are borne on panicles that are 3 to 6 cm long. These flowers bloom in late spring. The fruit is an oblong red berry, 7 to 10 mm in length and 3 to 5 mm in width, which ripens in late summer or autumn. The berries are edible but have a very sour taste and are rich in Vitamin C. The plant has both toxic and medicinal properties. While the fruits and seeds are safe for consumption, the rest of the plant is mildly poisonous. The primary active compound in the plant is berberine, which is known to have various therapeutic effects. In Europe, the berries are traditionally used to make jam. In southwestern Asia, particularly in Iran, the berries are used in cooking, such as for spicing rice dishes. Berberis vulgaris serves as an intermediate host for Puccinia graminis, the pathogen responsible for black rust, a serious fungal disease affecting wheat. As early as 1660, wheat farmers suspected barberry plants of spreading rust, but their claims were dismissed as superstitious by those who used the berries for jam-making. It was not until 1865 that the connection between barberry and wheat rust was scientifically confirmed. Due to the detrimental impact of this disease on wheat crops, the cultivation of European Barberry is prohibited in many regions.
